text.p: Luxembourg's Marc Girardelli, one of the greatest racers in the history of Alpine skiing, announced his retirement on Monday after doctors told him to quit or risk a life on crutches.
The five-times overall World Cup champion said he had wanted to complete this season and continue until the 1998 Nagano Olympics but his 33-year-old body, battered by injury, could stand no more.
"The only thing that I have to do now is announce my retirement," the Austrian-born all-rounder told a packed news conference at the world championships.
Girardelli said a downhill in Val d'Isere in December had done serious damage to his knee, although it had appeared otherwise at first and he had finished the race.
His last race was a downhill just before Christmas in Val Gardena when he came 57th out of 60 starters and he said that was the discipline he would miss the most.
"I know that I will never again have the chance to put the long skis on my legs again," Girardelli said.
He went to Munich to see specialists and increased speculation that he would retire when he failed to turn up in Sestriere last week to defend his combined title.
"Three doctors urged me to retire," he said. "They said I risked my future and could not guarantee that I might not have to walk on crutches for the rest of my life."

There was a sad irony in Girardelli's choice of venue in announcing his retirement. It was in Sestriere in 1989 that he had a crash during a super-giant slalom that almost killed him through internal bleeding diagnosed much later.
Since his first World Cup podium in Wengen in 1981 he has undergone major surgery 13 times and earned the nickname of "The Bionic Man" of skiing.
He won 46 races and captured 13 medals at championships and Olympics in a 17-year career.
Yet the proud and private, some would say dour, skier -- whose team was a one-man band dominated by his father Helmut -- never captured the crowd's imagination as others had.

Girardelli, who started the conference by thanking his sponsors one by one, admitted he had never been as popular as his rivals, particularly in his early years when he cut a solitary and often prickly figure on the piste.
"When I see the audience here I think maybe I should retire every week," he joked. "I never saw such a big crowd after any of my victories. It's a very emotional day for me."
"My fans are all over the world. They are not the kind who turn up with cowbells and banners. They are quieter, behind the television screens, in the shadows lets say," he said.
"But I knew they were there behind me."

Marc Hodler, president of the International Ski Federation, hailed Girardelli as a "great athlete, sportsman and personality" who could do more for the sport than thousands of ski clubs and hundreds of national federations.
"You are one of the great skiers who has been able to beat other great skiers in all four disciplines and make them look second best. You will not be forgotten," he said.
Girardelli gave few indications about his future, beyond saying that he wanted to study his options and undergo further education for a while before making further decisions.

Asked whether there was one thing he regretted in his career, Girardelli, who has a young son from a past relationship, said with a smile that it was failure to find "the girl of my dreams". Otherwise he had no complaints.

Of his choice to race for Luxembourg, which arose after a disagreement with the local officials in his native Vorarlberg when he was just starting out as a teenager, he said he considered himself a European above all.
